title: The earth, a dharamsaal
carry: the earth is a dharamsaal, a home for living rightly
tomorrow: before sunrise, someone on the porch is talking to the birds. who?

cards: Saturday, and the strip of dirt behind Arjan's building has more people in it than it's ever held. Arjan's mom is turning the soil. Mrs.
Haddad brought a bucket of coffee grounds and eggshells for compost. Bebe is directing everyone, mostly Harjit. Maya and Simran are setting chili seedlings and mint cuttings into one long bed.
Jasleen is in charge of the watering can, and takes the job very seriously. Nobody asked whose garden it is. It's just the ground, and everyone's on their knees in it.

teach.b: The Japji's last lines finish the family picture: air the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother. Earlier, in its thirty-fourth pauri on Ang 7, the Japji gives the earth another name.

teach.h: A DHARAMSAAL: A HOME FOR LIVING RIGHTLY.
teach.b: In paraphrase: among nights and seasons, air, water and fire, the One set the earth in place as a dharamsaal, a home for living rightly. So the ground isn't just under the practice. It is where the practice happens.
A mother feeds you; you plant, compost, and protect what feeds you back.
Now look at these two weeks from this garden. Welcome the stranger: a door with no name, then four cups. Friendship first, over bread.
Water for both sides, even for Cole. Honor the humble, at a night-shift table. Air is the guru, under an orange sky.
Water is the father, at the hose. And before all that, a freshman staring at his shoes at the bus stop. Today he's laughing with his little sister in the dirt.
Earth is the mother, and her lap is big enough for everyone kneeling in it.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji, which calls the earth the great mother and a dharamsaal, in morning prayer, and some gurdwaras and Sikh families plant trees and gardens as seva.

games.q: what does “earth is the mother” mean?
o: the ground that feeds us and the place to live rightly
the old name for the land around the Golden Temple
a goddess Sikhs pray to for a good harvest each spring

games.q: the earth week, and two weeks back — tap the pairs.
p: the earth, in the Japji's last lines
from the bus stop to the garden

s: the Japji calls the earth a dharamsaal, a home for living rightly
the thirty-fourth pauri, on Ang 7, in paraphrase.
'earth is the mother' means leaving nature completely untouched
a mother feeds you, and you tend her back: plant, compost, protect.
a garden only counts as seva if it's at the gurdwara
the Japji calls the whole earth a dharamsaal; the practice happens on the ground itself.

games.q: the city plans to pave the empty lot on your block. some neighbors, of several faiths, want a garden there. going by these two weeks, what fits best?
o: go to the meeting with your neighbors and offer to help start a shared garden.
post a complaint about the city online and leave it there.
let it go; the land belongs to the city, not to any of you.
games.why: earth is the mother: plant, compost, protect, together. friendship first, honor the humble, welcome the stranger, all in one garden bed.

practice: If you can, put both palms flat on the ground: soil, grass, a floor, whatever holds you up right now. Feel it take your weight without asking anything back.
Stay there for a few slow breaths, then think of one living thing you could plant or tend this season.

wordCard.voice: Earth is the mother. From the Japji's last lines: the ground that feeds us, the dharamsaal where we live rightly, tended by planting, compost and protection.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dharamsaal, a home for living rightly. The Japji gives the earth this name (Ang 7).

carryVoice: Two weeks in one line: the earth is a dharamsaal, a home for living rightly, and everyone fits in the great mother's lap. Fourteen days, from a bus stop to a garden bed.

sources.ref: Ang 8, Japji, closing salok ('maataa dharat mahat'), paraphrased
Ang 7, Japji, pauri 34 ('tis vich dharti thaap rakhi dharamsaal'), paraphrased
